en: Preface to the "Section on the Principle of Prajñā" from the Tenth Assembly of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Xuánzé of Xīmíng Monastery.
The "Section on the Principle of Prajñā" is intended to examine the essential purport of all the assemblies and to synthesize the accumulated chapters.
Regarding this ancestral lineage, he cast aside the verbal fish-trap to stir his profound regard and illuminated mental images to give rise to his discourse.
Thus, when observing where the treasures of virtue converge, the wisdom of the Vajra is supreme;
when basking in the brilliance of contemplative insight, the wisdom of the Perfect Mirror holds the position of honor.
Thus, ascending to the celestial palaces, he takes sovereignty as the manifestation of his mind;
opening the jeweled halls to the side, he relies upon mani-gems as the sign of his teaching.
Clarifying the supreme model of Prajñā, it serves as the profound treasury of myriad practices; therefore, one can gallop across the great earth and rest one’s staff upon the Supreme Vehicle.

Having attained the One to model the Truth, and blowing through the myriad things to discern the mundane, his practice and rank accumulated together, towering like a mountain of virtue rising in majestic prominence;
his phrases and meanings were perfected in their entirety, swallowing the ocean of teachings until it was clear and vast.

He gathers the vessel of true purity into the vast wheel; his nature is inscribed with the seal to form the pattern, and his wisdom is preeminent to manifest its substance. Thereafter, he enters the stage of consecration and don the gate of *dhāraṇī*; with a mind of quiescent extinction, he abides in the nature of equality. He washes away conceptual proliferation so that there is nothing to be said, and utterly abandons delusive thoughts so that there is nothing to be conceived. This is sufficient to cause joy and anger to share a single sentiment, and to view friend and enemy as equal.
Names are merely provisional, yet they share the profound depth of the Dharma-realm;
though obstructions and outflows have not yet been extinguished, they are equally distant from enlightenment.

Truly, the mind is concentrated and the purport is remote; the meaning is lucid and the phrasing is clear. When discussing principle, the principle is so profound it dwells within the center of the circle; when speaking of the ultimate goal, that goal is so vast it lies beyond the furthest reaches of the earth.

Although this is a single fascicle translated as a standalone work, it encompasses all its various parts; if one does not linger over this profound meaning and savor these words, how could one point toward the distant ford or seek out the wondrous and secret treasury?

The Tenth Chapter: The Section on the Principle of Prajñā. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat had perfectly accomplished all the Tathāgatas’ vajra-abiding wisdom of equality and various rare, supreme merits;

he had successfully obtained the jewel-crown initiation of all Tathāgatas and transcended the three realms; he had successfully attained the universal vajra-wisdom of all Tathāgatas and the Great Sovereignty of Avalokiteśvara; he had attained the seal of the great, wondrous wisdom that definitively establishes all dharmas of all Tathāgatas; and he had perfectly realized the seal of the ultimate emptiness and quiescence of the equality of all Tathāgatas.
Regarding all activities to be performed and those already performed, he had attained skillful mastery in accomplishing them all without exception.

All the various aspirations of sentient beings are fulfilled according to their needs, provided they are blameless; having well established themselves in the equality of the three times, they are eternally uninterrupted and inexhaustible.
Their vast and all-pervading nature of body, speech, and mind is like a vajra, equal to that of all Tathāgatas—unmoving and indestructible.

This Bhagavān dwells in the palace of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods at the summit of the desire realm—a place where all Tathāgatas constantly roam and which they all collectively praise as the Great Jewel Treasury Hall.
That palace was constructed of priceless *maṇi* jewels, adorned with an intermingling of various rare and wondrous treasures that reflected one another’s colors and emitted great radiance.
Precious bells and golden chimes were suspended everywhere; when stirred by a gentle breeze, they produced harmonious and elegant sounds.

It was further embellished with various ornaments such as exquisite canopies, silken banners, flowered pennants, colorful fly-whisks, precious beads, necklaces, and crescent or full-moon shaped decorations—objects cherished by the worthy sages and celestial seers.

He was accompanied by eight billion great bodhisattvas, all of whom were endowed with the gates of dhāraṇī, the gates of samādhi, and unimpeded, wondrous eloquence, as well as immeasurable virtues of this kind that could not be fully extolled even if one were to spend many kalpas doing so. Their names were: the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramuṣṭi, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāgaganagañja, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Citta-utpāda-dharmacakra-pravartaka, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvamāraparapravādin.

Thus, surrounded before and behind by a foremost assembly of eight million great bodhisattvas, he proclaimed the True Dharma—good in the beginning, middle, and end; skillful in its phrasing and meaning; pure, complete, and the holy life of total purity.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of the bodhisattvas, expounded the Dharma-gate of the Pure Principle of the Profound and Subtle Prajñā of All Dharmas; this gate is precisely the meaning of the term "bodhisattva."
What is called the meaning of the term "bodhisattva"?
It refers to the meaning of the term "supremely wondrous, blissful, and pure" as being the meaning of the term "bodhisattva."
The pure phrase-meaning of the eternal stillness of all views is the bodhisattva’s phrase-meaning;
the pure phrase-meaning of subtle, exquisite, and delightful joy is the bodhisattva’s phrase-meaning;
the pure phrase-meaning of the eternal cessation of craving is the bodhisattva’s phrase-meaning.
The phrase "purity through transcending the womb" is a phrase of the bodhisattva;
the phrase "purity through the adornment of all virtues" is a phrase of the bodhisattva;
the phrase "purity through the mind’s ultimate tranquility and ease" is a phrase of the bodhisattva.
The phrase "attaining the purity of great radiance" is a bodhisattva phrase;

the phrase "the purity of physical well-being and bliss" is a bodhisattva phrase; the phrase "the purity of verbal well-being and bliss" is a bodhisattva phrase; the phrase "the purity of mental well-being and bliss" is a bodhisattva phrase;

the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the aggregate of form" is a bodhisattva phrase; and the phrases "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness" are bodhisattva phrases.

The meaning of the phrase "the sense-base of the eye is empty, quiescent, and pure" is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the phrases "the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, quiescent, and pure" is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of the phrase "the sense-object of form is empty, quiescent, and pure" is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the phrases "the sense-objects of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are empty, quiescent, and pure" is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of the phrase "the eye-element is empty, quiescent, and pure" is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the phrases "the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty, quiescent, and pure" is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the realm of form" is the phrase of a bodhisattva; the phrases "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena" are the phrases of a bodhisattva.

The phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the eye-consciousness realm" is the phrase of a bodhisattva; the phrases "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness realms" are the phrases of a bodhisattva.

The phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of eye-contact" is the phrase of a bodhisattva; the phrases "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact" are the phrases of a bodhisattva.

The phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all sensations produced with eye-contact as a condition" is the phrase of a bodhisattva; the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all sensations produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions" is the phrase of a bodhisattva;

the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the earth element" is the phrase of a bodhisattva; the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements" is the phrase of a bodhisattva;

the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the noble truth of suffering" is the phrase of a bodhisattva; the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path" is the phrase of a bodhisattva.

The phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of causes and conditions" is a phrase for a bodhisattva; the phrases "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the immediately preceding condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition" are phrases for a bodhisattva;

the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of ignorance" is a phrase for a bodhisattva; the phrases "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death" are phrases for a bodhisattva;

the phrase "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the perfection of generosity" is a phrase for a bodhisattva; and the phrases "the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom" are phrases for a bodhisattva.

The meaning of the term "emptiness, stillness, and purity of suchness" is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva. The meaning of the terms "dharma-realm," "dharma-nature," "non-falsity," "unchanging nature," "equality," "nature free from birth," "dharma-constancy," "dharma-abiding," "the limit of reality," "the realm of space," and "the inconceivable realm—all of which are empty, still, and pure"—is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva.
The meaning of the terms "the four dhyānas, which are empty, still, and pure" is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva.
The meaning of the terms "the four immeasurables and the four formless absorptions, which are empty, still, and pure" is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva."

The meaning of the emptiness, tranquility, and purity of the four foundations of mindfulness is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the emptiness, tranquility, and purity of the four right endeavors, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path is the meaning of the bodhisattva;

the meaning of the emptiness, tranquility, and purity of the gate of liberation of emptiness is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the emptiness, tranquility, and purity of the gates of liberation of signlessness and wishlessness is the meaning of the bodhisattva;

the meaning of the emptiness, tranquility, and purity of the eight liberations is the meaning of the bodhisattva; and the meaning of the emptiness, tranquility, and purity of the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, and the ten totalities is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of the term "empty, quiescent, and pure" regarding the Stage of Utmost Joy is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva"; the meaning of the term "empty, quiescent, and pure" regarding the Stage Free from Defilement, the Radiant Stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage, the Manifest Stage, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, and the Cloud of Dharma Stage is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva";

the meaning of the term "empty, quiescent, and pure" regarding the Stage of Pure Observation is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva"; and the meaning of the term "empty, quiescent, and pure" regarding the Stage of the Spiritual Lineage, the Eighth Stage, the Stage of Attaining Vision, the Stage of Refinement, the Stage of Freedom from Desire, the Stage of Completion, the Stage of the Pratyekabuddha, the Stage of the Bodhisattva, and the Stage of the Tathāgata is the meaning of the term "bodhisattva."

The meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all *dhāraṇī* gates is the meaning of the Bodhisattva; the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all *samādhi* gates is the meaning of the Bodhisattva;

the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the five eyes is the meaning of the Bodhisattva; the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the six supernormal powers is the meaning of the Bodhisattva;

the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the ten powers of a Tathāgata is the meaning of the Bodhisattva; and the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, great equanimity, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha is the meaning of the Bodhisattva.

The meaning of the thirty-two marks being empty, quiescent, and pure is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the eighty secondary characteristics being empty, quiescent, and pure is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of the quality of non-forgetfulness being empty, quiescent, and pure is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the nature of constant equanimity being empty, quiescent, and pure is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) being empty, quiescent, and pure is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) being empty, quiescent, and pure is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all dharmas of ordinary beings is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all dharmas of stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

The meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas is the meaning of the bodhisattva; the meaning of the emptiness, quiescence, and purity of all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, specified and unspecified dharmas, outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas, mundane and supramundane dharmas is the meaning of the bodhisattva.

"Why is this? Because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, they are inherently detached; because they are detached, their intrinsic nature is quiescent; because they are quiescent, their intrinsic nature is pure; and because they are pure, the most excellent purity of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is realized."
"You should know that this Prajñāpāramitā is itself the meaning of the term 'bodhisattva'; all bodhisattvas should practice and study it.
After the Buddha had thus spoken this pure Dharma of the principle of the Prajñā of the Bodhisattva-meaning, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this profound and subtle Dharma-gate of the pure principle of the Prajñā of all dharmas and receive it with deep faith, until they sit upon the sublime seat of awakening, no obstacles or veils shall be able to defile them—namely, the obstacle of afflictions, the obstacle of karma, and the obstacle of retribution. Even if these are accumulated in great measure, they shall not be able to defile them."
Even if one has committed various extremely grave evil karmas, they will be easily extinguished, and one shall not fall into the miserable realms.

If one can receive and uphold this [teaching], reading and reciting it daily, practicing with diligent and uninterrupted effort, and reflecting upon it according to the principle, then in this very life, one will certainly attain the Vajra Samādhi of the Equality of All Dharmas. One will attain mastery over all dharmas and constantly experience all supreme and wondrous joys. After passing through sixteen births as great Bodhisattvas, one will certainly attain the nature of the Tathāgata-Vajradhara and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One again, based upon the characteristics of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*—the gateway to the manifest perfect awakening to the quiescent *dharmatā* of all Tathāgatas. That is to say:
"The gateway to the manifest perfect awakening to the equality of the vajra, because Great Bodhi is solid, indestructible, and like a vajra;
the gateway to the manifest perfect awakening to the equality of meaning, because the meaning of Great Bodhi is one;"
The gateway to the manifest perfect awakening to the equality of phenomena, because the nature of great enlightenment is pure;
the gateway to the manifest perfect awakening to the equality of all phenomena, because great enlightenment is non-conceptual with respect to all phenomena.
When the Buddha had thus fully awakened to the principle of the Prajñāpāramitā, the nature of which is such tranquility, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

“If there are those who hear these four gateways of the principle of the Prajñāpāramitā for full awakening, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and practice them, they shall—until they sit upon the sublime seat of enlightenment—be able to transcend all evil destinies and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, even if they have committed all manner of most grievous evil deeds.”

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the manifestation of Śākyamuni Tathāgata who subdues all unwholesome dharmas, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the profound principle of the Dharma-gate of Universal Excellence, which encompasses the equality of all phenomena within the Prajñāpāramitā. He said:
"Because the nature of desire is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of hatred is also free from conceptual proliferation;
because the nature of hatred is free from conceptual proliferation, the nature of delusion is also free from conceptual proliferation."
Because the nature of delusion is without conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), the nature of doubt is also without conceptual proliferation;
because the nature of doubt is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of all views is also without conceptual proliferation;
and because the nature of all views is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of arrogance is also without conceptual proliferation.
Because the nature of pride is without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) is also without conceptual proliferation;
because the nature of the envelopments is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of the stains of affliction (*kleśamala*) is also without conceptual proliferation;
because the nature of the stains of affliction is without conceptual proliferation, the nature of all evil karma is also without conceptual proliferation.
Because the nature of all evil karma is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of all karmic retributions is also free from conceptual proliferation;
because the nature of all karmic retributions is free from conceptual proliferation, the nature of all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) is also free from conceptual proliferation;
and because the nature of all defiled phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation, the nature of all pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) is also free from conceptual proliferation.
Because the pure nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the nature of all phenomena is likewise free from conceptual proliferation;
because the nature of all phenomena is free from conceptual proliferation, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is also free from conceptual proliferation.
When the Buddha had thus taught this *Prajñāpāramitā* principle of the Universal Conquest for the Subduing of All Evil, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there should be anyone who hears such a profound principle of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and with faith and understanding receives, maintains, recites, and practices it, even if they were to kill all sentient beings included within the three realms, they would not thereby fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts;

for by being able to subdue all afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and evil karma, they will always be born in the happy destinies and experience supreme bliss, practicing the conduct of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas and swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One again relied upon the characteristic of the Tathāgata of Innate Purity to proclaim for the sake of all bodhisattvas the profound principle of the Seal of the Wondrous Wisdom of Avalokiteśvara—the Dharma-gate of the Purification of the Equality of All Dharmas within the Prajñāpāramitā. He said:
"Because the intrinsic nature of all desire is pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the hatred of the world to be purified;
because the intrinsic nature of all hatred is pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the delusion of the world to be purified."
Because the intrinsic nature of all ignorance is pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the doubts of the world to be purified;
because the intrinsic nature of all doubts is pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the views and inclinations of the world to be purified;
because the intrinsic nature of all views and inclinations is pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the arrogance of the world to be purified.
Because all pride is by nature pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the fetters of the world to be purified;
because all fetters are by nature pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the defilements of the world to be purified;
because all defilements are by nature pure and supremely luminous, it can cause the unwholesome dharmas of the world to be purified.
Because all unwholesome dharmas are by nature pure and supremely luminous, they can cause the cycle of birth and death in the world to be purified;
because all births and deaths are by nature pure and supremely luminous, they can cause all phenomena in the world to be purified;
and because all dharmas are by nature pure and supremely luminous, they can cause sentient beings in the world to be purified.
Because the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is utterly luminous and pure, they can cause the omniscience of the world to be purified;
because the intrinsic nature of omniscience is utterly luminous and pure, it can cause the most supreme purity of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* in the world.
When the Buddha had thus taught this pure Dharma of the *Prajñāpāramitā-naya* of the Seal of Equal Wisdom (*samatājñānamudrā*), he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this pure *Prajñāpāramitā-naya*, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and cultivate it, then even though they dwell amidst the accumulation of all adventitious afflictions and defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion, they will remain unstained by any adventitious dust, defilements, or faults—just as a lotus flower is not soiled by them—and they shall always be able to cultivate the supreme conduct of a bodhisattva, swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the marks of the Tathāgata, the Supreme Lord of all the three realms, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the profound principle of the Dharma-gate of the Wisdom-Treasury, the Consecration of the Union of All Tathāgatas, which is the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā). He said:
"By bestowing the consecration of the worldly rank, one shall attain the fruit of the rank of Dharma-King over the three realms;
by bestowing the unsurpassed meaning of the supramundane, one shall attain the fulfillment of all aspirations."
By means of the unsurpassed gift of Dharma that transcends the world, one shall attain mastery over all phenomena;
if one gives worldly wealth, food, and so forth, one shall obtain happiness of body, speech, and mind;
and by giving various kinds of material wealth and the Dharma, one can swiftly bring the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) to full completion.
By upholding various pure prohibitions and precepts, one can swiftly bring the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) to fulfillment;
by practicing patience (*kṣānti*) in all matters, one can swiftly bring the perfection of patience to fulfillment;
and by cultivating diligence (*vīrya*) at all times, one can swiftly bring the perfection of diligence to fulfillment.
By practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) toward all objects, one can swiftly bring the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) to fulfillment;
by constantly cultivating sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding all phenomena, one can swiftly bring the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) to fulfillment.
When the Buddha had thus taught this *prajñāpāramitā* principle of the treasury of wisdom—the Dharma-gate of empowerment—he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this profound principle of the treasury of wisdom—the Dharma-gate of empowerment—and believe, understand, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will swiftly fulfill all bodhisattva practices and rapidly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the Tathāgata’s mark of the Wisdom-Seal (*jñāna-mudrā*) which sustains all Buddhas’ secret Dharma-gates, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the profound principle of the Vajra Dharma-gate of the Wisdom-Seal of Sustenance of All Tathāgatas within the Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
“By fully embracing the Vajra Body Seal of all Tathāgatas, one shall realize the Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas;
if one fully embraces the Vajra Speech Seal of all Tathāgatas, one shall attain mastery over all phenomena.”
If one fully embraces all the Tathāgatas’ vajra-mudrās of mind, one shall attain mastery over all meditative absorptions;
if one fully embraces all the Tathāgatas’ vajra-mudrās of wisdom, one will obtain the supreme and wondrous body, speech, and mind, which, like a vajra, are immovable and indestructible.
When the Buddha had thus spoken this Vajra Dharma of the Prajñāpāramitā Principle of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom Seal, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

“If there be anyone who hears this profound principle of the Wisdom Seal Vajra Dharma-gate, and with faith and understanding receives, maintains, recites, and practices it, they shall be able to accomplish all undertakings and will always be in harmony with all superior matters. Whatever supreme wisdom they wish to cultivate and whatever superior meritorious deeds they perform shall all be swiftly perfected. They shall obtain the most supreme purity of body, speech, and mind, which, like a vajra, is indestructible, and they shall quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the Tathāgata’s mark of all dharmas free from conceptual proliferation, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*, the Dharma-gate of the Wheel of Syllables, saying:
"All dharmas are empty, because they lack intrinsic nature;
all dharmas are signless, because they are detached from all signs."
All phenomena are wishless, because there is nothing to be wished for;
all phenomena are detached, because there is nothing to which they cling;
all phenomena are tranquil, because they are eternally extinguished.
All phenomena are impermanent, because their nature is eternally non-existent;
all phenomena are without bliss, because they are not worthy of being enjoyed;
all phenomena are without self, because they lack autonomy.
All dharmas are without purity, because they are free from the characteristics of purity;
all dharmas are unattainable, because their nature cannot be found through investigation;
all dharmas are inconceivable, because no such nature exists that can be conceived.
All phenomena are non-existent, for they are merely provisionally designated through the conjunction of various conditions;
all phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation, for their intrinsic nature is empty and quiescent, transcending all verbal expression;
all phenomena are pure by nature, for the intrinsic nature of the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is pure by nature.

When the Buddha had thus taught this Dharma-gate of the Wheel of Syllables for the Principle of Prajñā, which is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate of the Wheel of Syllables for the Principle of Prajñā, free from conceptual proliferation, and who believe, understand, uphold, recite, and cultivate it, they shall attain unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One again relied upon the Tathāgata-marks of the wheel-gathering of all Tathāgatas, and for the sake of the bodhisattvas, proclaimed the gate of the equality of the profound principle of entering the vast wheel of the *prajñāpāramitā*, saying:
"By entering the equality of the vajra, one is able to enter the nature-wheel of all Tathāgatas;
by entering the equality of meaning, one is able to enter the nature-wheel of all bodhisattvas."
They enter the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all phenomena;
they enter the equality of the aggregates (*skandha-samatā*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all aggregates;
they enter the equality of the sense bases (*āyatana-samatā*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all sense bases.
Entering the equality of the elements (*dhātu*), because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all elements;
entering the equality of the truths (*satya*), because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all truths;
entering the equality of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), because one is able to enter the wheel of the nature of all dependent originations.
They enter the equality of jewels, because they are able to enter the wheel of all jewel-natures;
they enter the equality of food, because they are able to enter the wheel of all food-natures;
they enter the equality of wholesome dharmas, because they are able to enter the wheel of all wholesome dharma-natures.
They enter the equality of non-virtuous phenomena, for they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all non-virtuous phenomena;
they enter the equality of determinate phenomena, for they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all determinate phenomena;
they enter the equality of indeterminate phenomena, for they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all indeterminate phenomena.
They enter the equality of all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all contaminated phenomena;
they enter the equality of all uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all uncontaminated phenomena;
they enter the equality of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all conditioned phenomena.
They enter the equality of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all unconditioned phenomena;
they enter the equality of worldly phenomena (*laukika-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all worldly phenomena;
they enter the equality of supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*), because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all supramundane phenomena.

They enter the equality of the dharmas of ordinary beings, because they are able to enter the wheel of the dharma-nature of all ordinary beings; they enter the equality of the dharmas of śrāvakas, because they are able to enter the wheel of the dharma-nature of all śrāvakas;
they enter the equality of the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, because they are able to enter the wheel of the dharma-nature of all pratyekabuddhas;
they enter the equality of the dharmas of bodhisattvas, because they are able to enter the wheel of the dharma-nature of all bodhisattvas.
They enter the equality of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, because they are able to enter the wheel of the Dharma-nature of all Tathāgatas;
they enter the equality of sentient beings, because they are able to enter the wheel of the nature of all sentient beings;
they enter all-equality, because they are able to enter the wheel of all natures.
When the Buddha had thus taught this entry into the equality of the principle of the vast wheel of *prajñā*, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this gate of the equality of the profound principle of the wheel-nature, and who believe, understand, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to skillfully awaken to and enter all states of equality, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the characteristics of the Tathāgata as the truly pure vessel-field for receiving all extensive offerings, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the supreme Dharma-gate of the profound principle of all offerings within the *Prajñāpāramitā*, saying:
“To give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is to extensively provide offerings to all Tathāgatas;
to uphold and protect the True Dharma is to extensively provide offerings to all Tathāgatas.”
They practice all the pāramitās, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas;
they practice all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas;
they practice all dhāraṇīs and samādhis, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
They practice all five eyes and six supernormal powers, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas;
they practice all meditative concentrations and liberations, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas;
they practice all loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, making extensive offerings to all Tathāgatas.
They cultivate all the unique qualities of the Buddhas and extensively provide offerings to the Tathāgatas;
they contemplate that all phenomena—whether permanent or impermanent—are unattainable, and extensively provide offerings to the Tathāgatas;
they contemplate that all phenomena—whether pleasant or painful—are unattainable, and extensively provide offerings to the Tathāgatas.
Contemplating all phenomena as either self or non-self, they find neither to be obtainable, yet they extensively make offerings to all Tathāgatas;
contemplating all phenomena as either pure or impure, they find neither to be obtainable, yet they extensively make offerings to all Tathāgatas;
contemplating all phenomena as either empty or non-empty, they find neither to be obtainable, yet they extensively make offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Contemplating that all phenomena—whether characterized by signs or signless—are ungraspable, one extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas;
contemplating that all phenomena—whether with aspiration or without aspiration—are ungraspable, one extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas;
contemplating that all phenomena—whether detached or non-detached—are ungraspable, one extensively makes offerings to all Tathāgatas.
Contemplating all phenomena, whether quiescent or non-quiescent, as being ultimately unapprehendable, one extensively makes offerings to the Tathāgatas;

one copies, hears, receives and maintains, recites, contemplates, and cultivates the profound Prajñāpāramitā, and widely proclaims and disseminates it for the sake of sentient beings; whether making offerings oneself or bestowing them upon others, one extensively makes offerings to the Tathāgatas.
When the Buddha had thus spoken this supreme dharma of the profound principle of the truly pure offering, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this supreme dharma gate of the Prajñāpāramitā principle of offering, and who believe, understand, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will swiftly fulfill all bodhisattva practices and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the characteristic of the Tathāgata who is capable of skillfully taming all beings, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Wisdom—the profound principle of taming sentient beings by embracing the secret wisdom of the *prajñāpāramitā*. He said:
"The equality of all sentient beings is the equality of anger; the tamed nature of all sentient beings is the tamed nature of anger;
the true dharma-nature of all sentient beings is the true dharma-nature of anger."
The *tathatā* (suchness) nature of all sentient beings is the *tathatā* nature of anger; the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) nature of all sentient beings is the *dharmadhātu* nature of anger;
the nature of all sentient beings being free from arising is the nature of anger being free from arising;
the nature of the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality) of all sentient beings is the nature of the *bhūtakoṭi* of anger; the nature of the original emptiness of all sentient beings is...
Anger is fundamentally emptiness; the signlessness of all sentient beings is the signlessness of anger;
the wishlessness of all sentient beings is the wishlessness of anger; the detachment of all sentient beings is the detachment of anger;
the tranquility of all sentient beings is the tranquility of anger; all sentient beings...
The unapprehendability of sentient beings is the very unapprehendability of anger; the non-existence of all sentient beings is the very non-existence of anger;

the inconceivability of all sentient beings is the very inconceivability of anger; the absence of conceptual proliferation in all sentient beings is the very absence of conceptual proliferation in anger; all sentient beings...
The nature of passion is the nature of vajra, and the nature of anger is the nature of vajra. Why is this so?

The true nature of the discipline of all sentient beings is itself unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; it is also the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), and it is the omniscient knowledge (sarvajñājñāna) of all Buddhas.
When the Buddha had thus spoken this Dharma-treasury of the profound principle of skillful subduement, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate of the Treasury of Wisdom on the Principle of Subduement Prajñā, and who believe, understand, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to subdue their own faults such as anger and wrath, and they will also be able to subdue all sentient beings. They will always be born in the happy realms and experience various sublime joys; in this present life, all enemies will give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness toward them; they will be able to skillfully practice the various bodhisattva deeds and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One, again relying on the Tathāgata’s characteristic of the nature of all phenomena that can be well-established as equality, proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the most supreme Dharma-gate of the profound principle of the nature of all phenomena within the Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
"Because the nature of all sentient beings is equal, the profound Prajñāpāramitā is also equal in nature;
because the nature of all phenomena is equal, the profound Prajñāpāramitā is also equal in nature."
Because the nature of all sentient beings is disciplined, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also disciplined by nature;
because the nature of all phenomena is disciplined, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also disciplined by nature;
because all sentient beings possess a real meaning, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* also possesses a real meaning.
Because all phenomena possess a real meaning, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* also possesses a real meaning;
because all sentient beings are *tathatā*, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also *tathatā*;
because all phenomena are *tathatā*, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also *tathatā*.
Because all sentient beings are the dharmadhātu, the profound perfection of wisdom is also the dharmadhātu;
because all phenomena are the dharmadhātu, the profound perfection of wisdom is also the dharmadhātu;
because all sentient beings are the dharmatā, the profound perfection of wisdom is also the dharmatā.
Because all phenomena are the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also the nature of phenomena;
because all sentient beings are the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also the limit of reality;
because all phenomena are the limit of reality, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also the limit of reality.
Because all sentient beings are primordially empty, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also primordially empty;
because all phenomena are primordially empty, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also primordially empty;
because all sentient beings are signless, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also signless.
Because all phenomena are signless, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also signless;
because all sentient beings are wishless, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also wishless;
because all phenomena are wishless, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also wishless.
Because all sentient beings are detached, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also detached;
because all phenomena are detached, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also detached;
because all sentient beings are quiescent, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also quiescent.
Because all phenomena are quiescent, the profound perfection of wisdom is also quiescent;
because no sentient beings can be apprehended, the profound perfection of wisdom also cannot be apprehended;
because no phenomena can be apprehended, the profound perfection of wisdom also cannot be apprehended.
Because all sentient beings are non-existent, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also non-existent;
because all phenomena are non-existent, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also non-existent;
because all sentient beings are inconceivable, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also inconceivable.
Because all phenomena are inconceivable, the profound perfection of wisdom is also inconceivable;
because all sentient beings are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the profound perfection of wisdom is also free from conceptual proliferation;
because all phenomena are free from conceptual proliferation, the profound perfection of wisdom is also free from conceptual proliferation.
Because all sentient beings are limitless, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also limitless;
because all phenomena (*dharma*) are limitless, the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is also limitless;
because all sentient beings possess karmic activity, one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* also possesses karmic activity.
"Because all phenomena possess functional activity (*karmakāritra*), one should know that the *prajñāpāramitā* likewise possesses functional activity.
Having thus spoken this most excellent Dharma of the profound principle of the equality of nature, the Buddha addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear such a supreme Dharma-gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* of equality, and who believe, understand, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it, they will be able to penetrate the profound *prajñāpāramitā* of the equal nature of phenomena. Their minds will be without obstruction toward all sentient beings, and they will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*)."

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the marks of the Tathāgata Sarvadhāraṇīgarbhadharma, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the profound principle of the supreme treasury-dharmagateway of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is the pervasive sustenance of all sentient beings. He said:
"All sentient beings are the tathāgatagarbha, because the self-substance of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is omnipresent;
all sentient beings are the vajragarbha, because they have been consecrated by the Vajragarbha."
All sentient beings are treasuries of the sublime Dharma, for all follow and turn according to the correct speech;
all sentient beings are treasuries of wondrous karma, for they rely upon the application of effort in all activities.
When the Buddha had thus taught this Dharma-door of the Supreme Treasury of the Profound Principle of Sustaining Sentient Beings, he addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

“If there are those who hear this Dharma-door of the Supreme Treasury of the Pervasive Prajñā-principle, and who believe, understand, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it, they shall be able to penetrate the dharmatā of the Supreme Treasury and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, further relying upon the marks of the Tathāgata of the ultimately boundless dharma, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the Vajra Dharma-gate of the Equality of the Ultimate Sustenance of the Meaning of Prajñāpāramitā, saying:
"Because the profound Prajñāpāramitā is boundless, all Tathāgatas are also boundless; because the profound Prajñāpāramitā is limitless, all Tathāgatas are also limitless."
Because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is of a single flavor, all phenomena (*dharma*) are also of a single flavor;
because the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is ultimate, all phenomena are also ultimate.
When the Buddha had thus spoken this Vajra Dharma of the Ultimate Principle that is Boundless and Limitless, he addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi and the others, saying:

"If there are those who hear this Vajra Dharma Gate of the Ultimate Prajñā Principle, and who believe, understand, receive, uphold, recite, and practice it, all obstructive dharmas will be entirely eliminated; they will certainly attain the nature of the Tathāgata-Vajradhara and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

At that time, the World-Honored One again, relying upon the aspect of the Tathāgata Samantaprabha, proclaimed for the sake of all bodhisattvas the *prajñāpāramitā* that attains the secret dharma-nature of all Tathāgatas and the non-conceptual nature (*niṣprapañcatā*) of all phenomena; the Vajra Dharma-gate of the Great Bliss Vajra Amogha-mantra; the supreme and foremost profound principle, the unsurpassed Dharma-gate of the initial, middle, and final stages. It is as follows:
"The supreme accomplishment of great passion and so forth brings about the supreme accomplishment of great bliss for the great bodhisattvas;
the supreme accomplishment of great bliss brings about the supreme accomplishment of the great awakening of all Tathāgatas for the great bodhisattvas."
The supreme accomplishment of the great awakening of all Tathāgatas brings about the supreme accomplishment of subduing all great Māras for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas;
the supreme accomplishment of subduing all great Māras brings about the supreme accomplishment of universal sovereignty over the three realms for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas;

and the supreme accomplishment of universal sovereignty over the three realms brings about the supreme accomplishment of ultimate great bliss for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas, enabling them to extract sentient beings from the realm of existence without exception and to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings. Why is this so?
Even unto the abodes of the cycle of birth and death, those of superior wisdom are able, by means of this peerless Dharma, to constantly benefit sentient beings and do not enter into nirvāṇa;
furthermore, through the skillful means of the *prajñāpāramitā*, they establish superior wisdom, skillfully accomplishing all pure activities and enabling all realms of existence to attain purity;
moreover, by means of desire and so forth, they subdue the world, universally and perpetually causing all realms of existence to be naturally subdued and purified.
Furthermore, just as a lotus flower is pure in form, color, and radiance, and cannot be defiled by any impurities,
so too do greed and the other [afflictions], while benefiting the world, remain forever unable to defile those who dwell amidst faults and transgressions.
"Furthermore, great greed and the like can attain purity, great bliss, great wealth, and sovereignty over the three realms; they are always able to remain steadfast in benefiting sentient beings.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke this divine mantra:
"Namo bhagavate... (Homage to the Blessed One).

*Sarvakālapratipannadaśe svāhā.* (12) *Svāhā.* (13) "This divine mantra is the mother of all Buddhas.

Those who can recite and uphold it will have all their sins extinguished, shall constantly behold all Buddhas, attain the knowledge of past lives, and swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
At that time, the Tathāgata again spoke this divine mantra:

*Namo bhagavate | Pratyamitāye | Tadyathā | Śrīye | Śrīye | Śrīye | Śrīye śive | Svāhā.* This divine mantra possesses great majestic power. Those who are able to receive and uphold it will have their karmic obstructions eliminated; they will maintain all the True Dharma they hear through dhāraṇī without forgetting it, and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, having spoken this mantra, the World-Honored One addressed Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and the others, saying:

“If there are sentient beings who, every morning at dawn, with a sincere mind, listen to and recite this profound principle of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this most supreme Dharma-gate, without interruption, all their evil karmic obstructions will be extinguished; all excellent joys and pleasures will constantly manifest before them; they will surely attain the manifestation of the Great Bliss Vajra-Non-empty Divine Mantra; they will ultimately fulfill the most supreme secret accomplishment of all Tathāgatas’ vajras; and before long, they shall attain the state of a Great Vajradhara and the nature of a Tathāgata.”

If there are classes of sentient beings who have not planted various roots of goodness under many Buddhas nor long since made great vows, they will be unable to hear, write down, recite, make offerings to, revere, contemplate, or practice this profound principle of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, this most supreme Dharma-gate.

Only those who have planted various roots of goodness under many Buddhas and long since made great vows will be able, at the very least, to hear even a single phrase or a single syllable of this profound principle and most supreme Dharma-gate, let alone be able to fully recite, receive, and uphold it!

If sentient beings were to make offerings, pay respect, honor, and praise as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in eighty *koṭī-nayuta* Ganges Rivers, they would then be able to fully hear this profound principle of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
In whatever region this sutra circulates, all devas, humans, asuras, and others should make offerings to it as they would to a stupa of the Buddha.
Wherever this sutra is placed upon the body or in the hand, all devas, humans, and others should pay homage to it with reverence.

If there are sentient beings who uphold this sutra for many koṭis of kalpas, they will attain the knowledge of past lives and constantly apply themselves with diligence to cultivate all wholesome dharmas; neither evil Māras nor externalists shall be able to detain them.

The Four Great Heavenly Kings and the other hosts of devas will constantly follow and protect them, never abandoning them for even a moment; they shall never meet with untimely death or unjust calamities.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will constantly provide protection and support, ensuring that at all times their goodness increases and their evils diminish.
One shall be reborn in accordance with one’s vows in all Buddha-fields, and until reaching enlightenment, shall never fall into the evil realms.
Any sentient beings who uphold this sutra will certainly obtain boundless benefits and merit; I now briefly describe but a small portion of these.

When the Bhagavat had finished speaking this sutra, Vajrapāṇi and the other great bodhisattvas, as well as the assembly of devas, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
